claim: METR's 2025 RCT found 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% SLOWER with AI tools, while having forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still believing afterward that AI sped them up by 20%.
quote: Developers expected AI to speed them up by 24% before the study. After experiencing the slowdown, they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%. 16 experienced developers participated... 246 total issues completed.

claim: METR explicitly cautions the 19% slowdown does NOT show AI fails to speed up most developers, is not evidence about novices or unfamiliar codebases, and may not generalize beyond their specific experienced-developer participant group.
quote: The authors explicitly state they do NOT provide evidence that: 'AI systems do not currently speed up many or most software developers'... findings may not apply to novice developers, unfamiliar codebases, or other contexts.

claim: In February 2026 METR redesigned its productivity experiment after finding selection bias (AI-optimistic developers refused to join no-AI conditions) and task cherry-picking, where 30-50% of developers avoided submitting tasks they thought AI would handle well, and called later subgroup speedup figures 'very weak evidence'.
quote: Between 30-50% of developers reported avoiding submission of tasks they believed AI could handle well... Later 2025 results showed speedups for some subgroups (-18% for returning developers, -4% for new ones), but researchers emphasize these figures are 'very weak evidence' due to selection effects.

claim: GitClear's 2025 analysis of 211M lines of code found code churn (revised within two weeks of commit) rose from 5.5% in 2020 to 7.9% in 2024, duplicated code blocks increased eightfold, and 2024 was the first year copy/pasted lines exceeded moved (refactored) lines.
quote: In 2024, 7.9% of all newly added code was revised within two weeks, compared to just 5.5% in 2020... the frequency of duplicated code blocks increased eightfold... 2024 was the first year when the number of copy/pasted lines exceeded the number of moved lines.

claim: The 2025 DORA report found AI now positively relates to delivery throughput (a reversal from 2024) but continues to have a NEGATIVE relationship with software delivery stability, and concludes AI amplifies existing team strengths and weaknesses rather than fixing them.
quote: AI adoption continues to have a negative relationship with software delivery stability... AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there. Strong teams use AI to become even better... Struggling teams will find that AI only highlights and intensifies their existing problems.

claim: Every AI code review vendor runs a self-favoring benchmark: Greptile claimed 82% recall on 50 PRs from 5 repos but scored only 45% when Augment Code re-evaluated the same repos; Qodo used LLM-generated synthetic bugs with unpublished ground truth, and competing vendors report incomparable F1 scores from 47.2% to 64% on different datasets.
quote: Each vendor runs their own benchmark, on their own dataset, and wins... Greptile: Reported '82% recall'... when Augment Code re-evaluated the same repos independently, Greptile's score dropped to 45%... F1 scores ranging from 47.2% to 64%, but each used different datasets, methodologies, and ground-truth construction approaches.

claim: The 'SWE-Bench Illusion' paper shows models identify buggy file paths with up to 76% accuracy using only issue text and no repository access (dropping to ~53% on outside-repo tasks), with 11.7-31.6% of instances showing verbatim memorization, concluding SWE-Bench scores reflect memorization not genuine problem-solving.
quote: State-of-the-art models achieved up to 76% accuracy identifying buggy file paths using only issue descriptions, without any repository structure or code access... 11.7% to 31.6% of test instances showed instance-level verbatim matching... reflects 'memorization rather than genuine problem-solving'.

claim: Independent audits of SWE-bench (SWE-Bench+) found 60.83% of successfully resolved issues involved solution leakage where the fix was provided or hinted in the issue text, and 47.93% of resolved issues passed only because of weak test cases.
quote: 60.83% of successfully resolved issues involve 'solution leakage', where solutions were either directly provided or indirectly hinted at in the issue report or comments... 47.93% of resolved issues were incorrectly marked as resolved due to patches passing weak test cases.
